The full upstream URL is embedded in the path, so the proxy knows where to forward without any config: ``` client baseURL before: https://api.openai.com/v1 client baseURL after: http://localhost:8787/bili/https://api.openai.com/v1 ``` For more per-client configuration examples, see the web UI guide at [http://localhost:8787](http://localhost:8787). **Verify.** With the proxy running and your config saved, check it answers and that your first real request shows compression activity in the log: ```bash # Health check (proxy up + where it forwards) curl -s http://localhost:8787/__bili/health # → {"ok":true,"upstream":"https://api.anthropic.com"} # Live session stats (after a real request) curl -s http://localhost:8787/__bili/stats ``` Then send one message from your client and watch the log (`~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log`, also printed to stderr). You should see a `processTurn` line per request, and once the conversation grows, `[acp-usage] round N input=X cached=Y (cache hit Z%)` + a `compress` event. ### Client deep dives Everything that doesn't fit in one Quickstart line — how each client's lanes attach, what gets written where, and known limitations — lives in **[docs/clients.md](docs/clients.md)**: dsh · Kimi Code · Hermes · ZCode · Gemini family (Gemini CLI / iFlow CLI / Qwen Code / Antigravity) · cert-MITM clients that never compress (CONNECT blind tunnels, #897) · unrecognized endpoints going direct (#1290) · OpenCode (launcher / native / pure proxy, `/acp` status & rules, legacy opencode-acp sessions #920). ## From source (development) > **Risk:** `master` is the development branch and can be broken at any moment — unreleased changes, failing builds, unverified fixes. Unless you are patching the code or testing an unreleased fix, install a release with npm as above. ```bash git clone https://github.com/ranxianglei/billion-context.git cd billion-context npm ci npm run build npm link bili --version ``` After `npm link`, `bili` works from any directory. ## FAQ **How do I check my cache hit rate?** Don't dig through logs — `/acp-cache` prints a **text summary report right in the client**, headed by a clickable **Web UI link**: open it for the web version of the session page — the cache hit-rate **line chart** plus per-break **attribution**: ![web session page: cache hit-rate chart + attribution](docs/cache-web-session.en.png) The report has four blocks that pin things down at a glance: **GRAND LEDGER** (totals + hit% with an explicit `HEALTHY` verdict; misses decomposed into new content / compress re-pay / upstream-ttl-or-client-rewrite) · **FOLD ECONOMICS** (per-fold economics: net tokens saved, paid-back verdicts) · **LINE ITEMS** (anomalies only: hit<85% or miss≥5000). Rule of thumb: **compression itself costs ≤2%** — a healthy session sits at **95–97%**. When you see less, the attribution tells you which of the usual suspects it was, in this order: ① upstream cache TTL expiry (shows up as stable-prefix misses — the top-spikes line names idle times), ② a model switch, ③ a bili bug (report it with the page attached), ④ other/unknown. `/acp-cache [full]` lists every fold & line; same report over Since #1535 the report ends with a `MODEL SWITCHES` section: a mid-session model change invalidates the provider's prefix cache, so the whole stable prefix is re-billed on the next request — each switch's unexplained residual (its `ttl` bucket minus new content) is charged to the switch instead of masquerading as TTL expiry; per-event `from → to`, hit %, and attributed tokens are listed (`full` lists every event, the summary the last 8), and the web sessions table gains a matching model-switch column. Since #2131 the same machinery fingerprints the outbound credential (a 12-hex sha256 of the `authorization`/`x-api-key`-family headers — the raw key is never stored) and attributes a **key switch** — the relay behind a stable URL rotated to a different account — in a dedicated `KEY SWITCHES` section, a `key switch:` line in `CACHE INVALIDATION`, and a 🔑 badge in the web sessions column. HTTP: `GET /__bili/cache-report`; the raw per-request `[acp-usage]` lines still land in the log file for deep dives. **What does `/acp` show?** In clients with the native plugin (opencode, dsh, hermes), `/acp` renders the ACP status panel of the current conversation straight from the proxy (session, blocks, compressible ranges, usage); before the first model request it shows an idle notice instead. `/acp-cache [full]` prints the cache report above. **Can I query sessions and config over the web?** Yes — open [http://localhost:8787](http://localhost:8787): an overview dashboard, session list with per-session detail, live logs, a config editor, and an upstream connectivity test. A Blog view renders notes and long-form articles inside the panel itself — bundled with the install, refreshed from GitHub master on a ~1-hour throttle while online (fail-soft to the bundled copy when offline); the full library also lives on GitHub Pages. Everything else is also plain JSON for scripting (`/__bili/stats`, `/__bili/sessions`, `/__bili/config`, …). **When does compression happen?** It is model-driven: the injected context tools are called by the model as context grows, gentle growth nudges (~50K-token steps by design, adjustable via `compress.nudgeGrowthTokens`) prompt it along the way, and preflight fires as a hard backstop when the input alone exceeds the window (#470). Watch it live with `/acp` or the web UI. **Does compression shrink my client's own conversation file?** No — the most common surprise in very long sessions (#5796). Compression shrinks **what is sent to the model**: every outgoing request is rebuilt from live blocks plus summaries, so the wire stays small however long the conversation runs. The client's stored history is user data — bili never rewrites it. On dsh the host's auto-compaction is additionally disabled while bili is active (two compressors must not fight over one history, #1772/#2474/#3354), so the host-side file grows with every turn: each turn takes longer as it grows (measured: tens of seconds per turn at ~30K messages, #5796), and the practical convergence path is to **start a new session** when it gets heavy. The web session list badges sessions at 5,000+ requests (长会话/slow) as a reminder that this point has been reached. **Why does the first compaction wait until ~200k?** Compaction does not trigger on absolute window position but on growth intervals: by default the first soft compaction fires 50k tokens past the boot content (`compress.nudgeGrowthTokens`, flat and window-independent). With a boot around 100k — or with the growth step set to ~100k — the first compaction may wait until ~200k. To make it fire earlier: 1) trim the system prompt, disable unneeded tools, prune skills; 2) lower `compress.nudgeGrowthTokens` to ~50k; 3) enable lean mode. Worked example in [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#why-the-first-compaction-waits-until-200k). **Is bili transparent? How do I turn it off?** Unrecognized endpoints forward unchanged ([docs/clients.md](docs/clients.md)), and every mode reverses cleanly: `bili plugin remove ` for native installs, stop using the launcher command / env vars / `/bili/` prefix for the other two — traffic goes direct again immediately. **Can I combine bili with a model-routing gateway (e.g. [magpie](https://github.com/yetone/magpie))?** Yes — point the client at bili, and point bili at the gateway through the `/bili/` prefix, which embeds the gateway's absolute URL: `http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425…`. Example: Claude Code → `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425` + `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=magpie`; OpenAI-style clients → `OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1` (+ `OPENAI_API_KEY=magpie`). Compression happens *before* routing — every request that reaches any account in the gateway's routing groups is already compressed. Credentials stay in the gateway: the client's dummy key rides through untouched, and real keys never touch bili. Caveats: ① an account switch mid-conversation invalidates the provider's prefix cache — inherent to multi-account routing, not bili (watch it in the `KEY SWITCHES` section of `/acp-cache`); ② routed model names are opaque to bili's window lookup — declare their context windows under the providers key `http://127.0.0.1:3425` via `models..context`, or they run on the fallback window (route-miss warning, #2317); ③ if the relay rejects bili's Anthropic-lane `cache_control` stamps, set `compat.noCacheControl`; ④ loopback gateways work out of the box; a gateway on a private non-loopback address may additionally need `network.allowPrivateHttpProviders` (#2984); ⑤ for Claude Code native plugin mode (`bili plugin install claude`), set `BILI_CLAUDE_UPSTREAM=http://127.0.0.1:3425` before install so the managed block wraps the relay into `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (or configure `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425` directly; `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` both accepted, #5369). Verified end-to-end over all three wires (OpenAI Chat / Responses / Anthropic Messages, including cross-protocol conversion), #4433. **Does this work with [opencodex](https://github.com/lidge-jun/opencodex) (`ocx`) — the local Codex/Claude Code gateway with a ChatGPT account pool?** Same pattern: point the client at bili, and point bili at ocx through the `/bili/` prefix — OpenAI-style clients (chat completions and Responses, e.g. Codex) → `OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:10100/v1`; Anthropic-style clients → `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:10100`. A dummy key value satisfies clients that require one; it rides through untouched. Keep bili *in front of* ocx rather than behind it: ocx owns the provider credentials and the account pool at its final hop, so only this order keeps compression and pooling working together. Loopback needs no key between the two (ocx's default loopback bind reads no token); a non-loopback bind takes `OPENCODEX_API_AUTH_TOKEN` plus the `x-opencodex-api-key` header per its docs. Request models by ocx's `provider/model` id so routing is deterministic; as with any gateway, routed ids are opaque to bili's window lookup (declare them via `models..context`) and a mid-session account rebind invalidates the prefix cache (watch `KEY SWITCHES` in `/acp-cache`). Verified end-to-end over all three wires (OpenAI Chat / Responses / Anthropic Messages), bili 0.1.212 × ocx 2.97.0. **Where are logs and session data stored?** Log: `~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log` (also mirrored to stderr); session state: `~/.local/share/billion-context/` (XDG-overridable; Windows AV exclusion #362, opt-in cleanup #1082) — full paths in [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md). ## Running the proxy ### Running in Docker A `Dockerfile` ships at the repository root — it installs the published npm package at build time (the tested artifact; nothing is compiled in the image) and runs the proxy as a service: ```bash docker build -t billion-context . docker run -d --name bili -p 8787:8787 \ -v bili-config:/root/.config/billion-context \ -v bili-data:/root/.local/share/billion-context \ -v bili-cache:/root/.cache/billion-context \ -v bili-state:/root/.local/state/billion-context \ billion-context ``` Then point clients' baseURL at `http://:8787/bili/…` exactly like Option 3 above. - **Base:** `node:24-slim` — uses the builtin `node:sqlite` storage engine directly (no native-addon download). Don't switch to Node 20 bases: the self-downloaded SQLite engine requires Node ≥ 22 and crashes under 20 (#3341). - **Updates:** in-container self-update is **off by default** (`ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0`) — the sanctioned update channel for a containerized copy is rebuilding/pulling a newer image; an in-place self-update would be silently reverted to the image version on the next recreate. Opt back in with `-e ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=1`; pin a release at build time with `--build-arg BILI_VERSION=0.1.197` (default `latest`). - **Data:** the four mounted dirs hold config, session state, update throttle/lock + cached SQLite engine, and logs respectively. Mount volumes or bind mounts so they survive container replacement; the image also declares them as `VOLUME`s so even a bare `docker run` keeps them out of the container layer. - **Security:** the container listens on `0.0.0.0:8787` so clients outside it can connect — there is **no authentication**, so expose the port only on a trusted network (same caveat as `--host 0.0.0.0` below). The web UI and `/__bili/*` JSON endpoints work unchanged through the mapped port. - **Healthcheck:** the image ships a `HEALTHCHECK` probing `/__bili/health` on 8787 via node's builtin fetch (no curl needed in the slim base); if you override the listen port, remember the probe stays pinned to 8787. ### Flags ```bash bili --port 9000 # change listen port bili --host 0.0.0.0 # listen on all interfaces (see host note below) bili --debug # verbose logging (also: set "debug": true in config) bili --passthrough # forward without compression (smoke-test mode) bili --config ~/my-bili.json # use a different config file bili update # check & install a newer version now (bypasses throttle) bili doctor --fix # converge drifted dsh profile ledgers (manifest spec / lockfile record / bundle copy) to the on-disk version (#3496) bili --no-auto-update # disable self-update for this run bili --auto-restart-on-update # self-restart when a new version is installed (default off) bili --bin /path/to/client # launcher: spawn this exact client binary instead of auto-detecting (env BILI_CLIENT_BIN) ``` Flags override env vars and the config file. `bili --help` lists them all. ### Remote agents (`--host`) By default the proxy binds `127.0.0.1` and only accepts loopback connections. To serve agents on other machines: `bili --host 0.0.0.0` (or your LAN IP); remote agents point their model `baseURL` at `http://:/bili/…`. - MITM-mode `CONNECT` then also accepts remote clients — for **whitelisted model hosts only**. Blind tunnels to arbitrary hosts stay loopback-only, so the proxy can never be used as an open relay. - `/bili/` destination admission (#409): the proxy itself and link-local/metadata addresses are always denied; loopback/private destinations are allowed for local clients (self-hosted upstreams) and denied for remote clients unless listed in `BILI_TUNNEL_ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`host` or `host:port`, comma-separated). One exception (#1073): a **local** client relaying a management path (`/__bili/*`, `/__acp/*`) to a **loopback IP-literal** destination is forwarded unmarked; remote peers and hostname destinations keep the internal tunnel marker unconditionally, and management paths stay unreachable through the tunnel even via NAT hairpin. An absolute-form request addressed to the instance's own endpoint on a management path is served locally instead of tunneled (a forward-proxy-style health probe gets a real answer). - There is **no authentication**: only do this on a trusted LAN or behind a firewall. The `/__bili/` management endpoints remain loopback-only. A startup `[security]` warning reminds you of the above. ### Debugging `bili --debug` (or env `ACP_DEBUG=1`, or `"debug": true` in config — flag > env > config) logs every `processTurn` (tag counts, token usage), the nudge decision (growth/usage/pendingT1/shouldInject), client headers, and SSE rewrites. ### Log file All logs tee to `~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log` by default (XDG state dir) and still print to stderr. Override with `"logFile"` in config or `ACP_LOG_FILE` (`off` disables the file). Auto-rotates at 10 MB (`bili.log.old`). Per-request cache-hit stats log as `[acp-usage] round N input=X cached=Y (cache hit Z%)` so you can measure prefix-cache health directly from the log. ### Connection lifecycle tuning (#1982) Client-facing connections close gracefully after the final response: when the proxy initiates the close (`Connection: close`), it waits up to `BILI_POST_RESPONSE_LINGER_MS` (default `5000`) for the client's close signal before releasing the socket, so pooled clients see a clean EOF instead of a possible RST from racing bytes. Related knobs: `BILI_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT_MS` (idle-reap budget, default `5000`) and `BILI_CLIENT_ERROR_BACKSTOP_MS` (terminal backstop for the error-drain path, default `30000`) — full semantics in [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#environment-variables). ### Self-update The proxy checks npm on startup and every 3 minutes; a newer version is installed in place and a notice is logged — **restart `bili` to pick it up**, unless you enable opt-in self-restart (`--auto-restart-on-update` flag, env `ACP_AUTO_RESTART_ON_UPDATE=1`, or `"autoRestartOnUpdate": true` in config — default OFF): with zero in-flight requests it verifies the new install, stops accepting connections, drains, spawns a replacement on the same port, and exits once it accepts connections (clients reconnect automatically; session state survives on disk). Safety gates: zero in-flight through the drain window, an install sanity check before re-exec, and a 10-minute cooldown marker so a flapping version can never loop-restart; any failure resumes the original listener and falls back to the plain reminder. **Staggered rollout (#3619):** a discovered version is not applied immediately by automatic updates. Each instance draws ONE random moment inside a delay window (built-in default **15 min – 48 h**) and upgrades when it arrives; the drawn moment is persisted, so restarts never re-roll. Fleet upgrades therefore spread across the window instead of completing within minutes of a release, leaving time to catch a bad release mid-rollout (#3401/#3600/#3394). The window plus emergency controls live in a public policy file (`auto-update-policy.json` in this repo, fetched anonymously with ETag caching): `hold` freezes automatic upgrades fleet-wide, `blocked` skips listed versions, `pinned` sets an upgrade ceiling. Fail-open by design — an unreachable or malformed file simply falls back to local defaults, and the file can steer timing/skip/pin only, never what gets installed. Per-machine exits: manual `bili update` bypasses `hold`/stagger (still respects `blocked`/`pinned`), `"staggerMinDelayMs": 0` + `"staggerMaxDelayMs": 0` (or `BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MIN_MS`/`BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MAX_MS`) restore legacy immediate upgrades, and `ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0` disables auto-updates entirely. Full format and semantics: [docs/configuration.md → `update`](docs/configuration.md#update). While the running process is behind the on-disk install ("stale"), the web UI shows a banner (running vs installed version, auto-restart state) and `GET /__bili/status` returns `{version, diskVersion, stale, autoRestartOnUpdate, advisory, updatePolicy, inFlight}` for scripting (`advisory` is the active critical-defect entry or `null`, see below; `updatePolicy` reports the #3619 rollout state — policy source, `hold`/`pinned`/`blocked`, and the pending staggered upgrade with its due time). Disable permanently via `"autoUpdate": false` in config or `ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0`. In **plugin mode** (`bili opencode` / `bili pi` / `bili dsh` — the proxy runs embedded in a long-lived host), "restart bili" means restarting the **host**: the embedded process cannot exit on its own, so a host left open keeps serving whatever code it started with, silently missing every fix auto-update reports as installed (#1603). Enable `--auto-restart-on-update` to have it self-restart at a safe point, or run `/acp` (OpenCode hosts today — pi/dsh coverage tracked in #2084) — the status panel appends a one-line staleness warning (running vs installed version) whenever the on-disk install is ahead of the live process. Auto-update only ever replaces disk files and (optionally) the proxy process; **injected code inside the host process only takes effect after the host itself restarts** — so if the injection breaks at runtime mid-session (a disposed agent scope, a disabled plugin), model traffic goes direct and uncompressed until then. Since #3581 this state is visible instead of silent: the web UI shows a "takeover broken" banner (agent + refusal count) whenever a plugin reports its attribution gate degraded while no session is live, and `GET /__bili/status` / `/__bili/overview` expose the per-agent `attribution` state (`ok`/`none`/`threw`, refusal count, first-refusal timestamp). Background lanes that are agentless **by design** (e.g. dsh's title-generation sidecar) never carry an initiator, so their small one-shot calls go direct by definition; under the #3651 contract these normal interceptions are NEVER reported and therefore can never raise the banner. The banner fires only when the attribution lookup itself throws (an internal host error, e.g. a disposed agent scope), and then names what failed: the thrown error text, the masked endpoint, when the episode started, how many requests went uncompressed, the remedy (restart the host process), plus copy/submit-diagnostics buttons that prefill a GitHub issue. **Update visibility is silent by default since v0.1.183 (#1977):** routine/recommended releases no longer render an update line on the `/acp` panel footer or in `acp_status` — only a `critical`-tier release surfaces there (`CRITICAL UPDATE READY/AVAILABLE`). The standing ways to check an installed-but-not-restarted release are the stale cues above: web UI banner, the `/acp` one-line warning, and `GET /__bili/status`. Deliberately no always-on nag; the advisory channel (#1481) remains the only auto-visible critical path. When an install keeps failing (unwritable or host-managed dir, network error, …), auto-update no longer re-downloads and retries on every 3-minute cycle forever. After three consecutive failures it backs off exponentially (5 min → 10 → 20 …, capped at 6 h), logs a one-time actionable hint (fix permissions / npm prefix, reinstall user-level, or disable via `"autoUpdate": false` / `ACP_AUTO_UPDATE=0`), and logs nothing further about the failure while cooling down (no download, no retry line); it resumes as soon as the failure clears or a different version is targeted (#1603). The same bounded retry now covers the **owner-managed lanes** the global self-update drives instead of writing the copy itself — the dsh desktop in-place copy, the dsh profile bundles, and pi's npm copy (#2192). Each lane keeps its own failure streak keyed by lane + target version, so a persistently broken desktop layout no longer re-downloads the full tarball every cycle (up to ~480 downloads/day per affected machine before the fix); three strikes arms the same exponential cooldown, and the one-time hint names the failing lane and its manual fix (`dsh plugin --profile add …`, `pi update --extension …`, or recreate the desktop profile). Host-managed instances additionally check on their own slower cadence — 30 minutes plus up to 15 minutes of jitter, tracked under a separate throttle marker — instead of consuming the global 3-minute budget. Failure streaks are shared across every bili process on the machine through a small state file in the cache dir (`.install-backoff.json`), so several running instances don't each burn their own retry budget; a clean `bili plugin update` disarms the dsh profile lane immediately. The file is written atomically (tmp+rename) and every writer merges with what is already on disk, so concurrent instances cooperate instead of overwriting each other's streaks; long-lived processes re-read it when it changes, so a manual disarm by one copy is visible to the others on their next check. It is fail-safe in the retry direction — a corrupt file or jumped clock is dropped, never allowed to silence a lane for long. `bili plugin update` clears the dsh-profile lane's key; a repaired desktop lane clears its own key on its next successful in-place refresh. ### Stale local DNS after a network/VPN change (#5224) A **long-lived** standalone proxy can keep holding stale OS-resolver state after a WSL/VPN/TUN topology change — the process caches its system resolver and libuv's `getaddrinfo` does not re-read `/etc/resolv.conf` on its own. Symptom: every model request through the `/bili/` tunnel answers HTTP 502 `tunnel_destination_denied` with detail `unresolvable`, even though a freshly started `bili` resolves the same host fine at that moment and `curl` from a new shell works. Either remedy clears it: - **Restart the proxy process** — a fresh process re-reads the system resolver. In the launcher lanes and the dsh web-profile lane the proxy is a *separate registered* process (the instance registry), so restarting only the client/host re-adopts the same wedged proxy and does **not** help — you must stop and relaunch the proxy itself. (In embedded plugin mode the proxy runs inside the host, so restarting the host *does* clear it.) - **Route egress through an upstream proxy** — `-F http://` or `BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY=… BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY_MODE=auto`: the destination is then resolved remotely by that proxy, so bili never consults its own (stale) resolver for admission. ### Critical-defect advisories (forced updates) Independent of auto-update (#1481): even with `autoUpdate` off, the proxy polls a small companion npm package (`billion-context-advisories`, published by CI from this repo's [`advisories/`](advisories/) directory) on the same 3-minute cadence. Each advisory names a semver range of broken versions (`affected`), the exact version to install (`target` — which may be *older* than the current one, i.e. a rollback), and a user-facing `reason`. When the local version falls inside `affected`, bili force-installs `target` through the self-updater's full safety chain (cross-process lock, backup + verify + rollback; source checkouts and host-managed installs are refused with manual instructions instead) and warns prominently: a one-time `[advisory] ⚠️ …` log line per process per advisory id, a banner on the web UI showing the reason and the exact manual upgrade command, and the active entry under `advisory` in `/__bili/status`. The check is fail-open by design: an unreachable or malformed advisory source only produces a warning — model traffic is never blocked by it. Disable via config (`"advisoryCheck": false`) or env (`BILI_ADVISORY_CHECK=0`); point at a custom document with `"advisoryUrl"` / `BILI_ADVISORY_URL`. **Announcements** (#5548) — distinct from the defect advisory above, three sources feed the web-UI banners, and equal ids shadow in the order **local file > remote feed > built-in**: (1) *built-in* one-time notices rendered from the UI i18n strings; (2) *local* — drop JSON files into `/announcements/*.json` (`~/.config/billion-context/announcements/` by default) and they render automatically: bilingual records with kind-derived color, npm-style `versions` targeting (`>=a.b.c`, `^`, `~`, `[lo hi]`, `||` lists), `percent` grey rollout, time windows, and per-kind priority — one bad file disables only itself; (3) *remote* — this repo's master branch [`announcements/remote.json`](announcements/remote.json) (CI-linted on every PR), fetched on the ~3-minute watcher cadence, whose last-known-good snapshot survives restarts and outages while malformed pushes are rejected; unreachable installs (firewalls) point `"remoteAnnouncementsUrl"` / `BILI_ANNOUNCEMENTS_URL` at a relay mirror of the same document. Dismissal follows each record's declared mode: `persistent` (default, content-addressed — editing a notice shows it again), `instance` (this process run only), or `always` (renders without a close button). Dismissing a built-in intro notice is recorded per install in bili's unified storage (SQLite by default; the MySQL backend works too), so it survives restarts — the old `upgrade-notices.json` state file remains only as fallback on legacy-only installs without a unified sidecar. The official feed currently ships an empty entry list. ## Configuration The full configuration reference — config file location, top-level keys, providers, compression tuning, environment variables — lives in **[docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md)**. ### Config file One JSON document at `~/.config/billion-context/billion-context.json` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/billion-context/`; override the path with `BILI_CONFIG_FILE`). Precedence when several sources set the same knob: **CLI flag (where one exists) > env var > config file > built-in default** — every env var keeps working as the override tier. What's inside (details in docs/configuration.md): - `providers` — per-provider routing table: upstream override, model context windows, per-provider/model compress tuning, wire-protocol declaration, compaction opt-in. - `compress` — three-level compression tuning (global → provider → model): thresholds, nudge cadence, preservation rules, prompts, tiers. - Server-level blocks — process-wide behavior, including the #2030 additions: `network` (timeouts / retry / keep-alive / preflight cadence), `persist` (session persistence format + tail), `sessions` (cap + GC policy), `update` (registry mirror + check interval), `diagnostics` (dumps, render-tag mode, injection switches), `fakeCompletion`, plus scalars `codexCompact` / `ccrRetrievalTtlMs` / `decompressTmpCap` and extensions `mitm.handshakeTimeoutMs`, `compat.noCacheControl`, `compat.keepResponseId`. Minimal example: ```json { "network": { "upstreamTimeoutMs": 900000 }, "persist": { "zstd": true }, "sessions": { "gc": { "enabled": true, "maxAgeDays": 14 } } } ``` Knobs people look for first: - **Upstream proxy (firewall/GFW)** — routing the proxy's own outbound traffic through v2rayA/clash: full resolution order, empty-string = explicit direct, SOCKS5 rejection, both egress paths, and the `mitm://` vs `https://` key schemes live in [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) (Server Settings → `proxy`; Providers → key schemes). - **Wire-compat role rewrite (`compat.roles`)** — an upstream that rejects the `developer` role? Covered by [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) (Server Settings → `compat`) — including the learn-on-failure auto-fix that needs no configuration at all. - **Signed upstreams (body-covering signatures)** — a gateway whose requests carry a body-covering signature (CodeArts APIG's `SDK-HMAC-SHA256`, or gateway-invented headers like `x-ofm-signature`): the built-in scheme re-signs transparently on dsh; every other detected scheme is ALWAYS refused locally — signed requests are either re-signed+compressed or refused, never passed through unsigned — and bili keeps reminding at startup and in the web UI until it ships the scheme's re-signer (#1884/#2090). Detection rules, per-scheme overrides, and `BILI_RESIGN` / `BILI_RESIGN_PASSTHROUGH` / `BILI_CODEARTS_REF` live in [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) (Server Settings → `resign`). ### Pi built-in subagents Using `bili pi` or the native pi plugin (`bili plugin install pi`) includes built-in subagent support, enabled by default: `acp_delegate`, `acp_delegate_wait`, and `acp_delegate_cancel`. This additional tool surface is specific to pi. **Keep only one subagent implementation enabled.** If you use the built-in support, remove or disable other pi subagent plugins (for example, `pi-subagents` or a separately installed `billion-context-pi-subagents`) in both user and project settings to avoid overlapping tools, prompts, or behavior. If you prefer another subagent plugin, disable the built-in support instead. A `pi-subagents` install at either scope (project or user) makes the built-in delegate stand down automatically by default — a user-scope install loads in every project, so the guard applies there too (#5637); set `delegate.forceEnable` to keep `acp_delegate` alongside it. To disable the built-in subagents while keeping context compression, merge this into `~/.config/billion-context/billion-context.json` (or the file selected by `BILI_CONFIG_FILE`), preserving your other settings: ```json { "pi": { "subagents": false } } ``` Restart pi and start a new session for the change to take effect. This disables the three delegate tools, their system-prompt section, and the fleet keyboard shortcut; context compression remains enabled. It does not disable independently installed subagent plugins. More options: [subagent configuration](docs/configuration.md#pi). ## How sessions work The proxy keys compression state on **the conversation value the client itself provides, verbatim** (`src/session-id.ts`) — no hashing, no protocol/upstream/API-key dimensions (those mutate mid-conversation and orphaned state exactly when users kept talking, #280/#286). The id stays inside the proxy (state store, persistence, UI label); it is never sent upstream. Where the value comes from, first hit wins: the plugin's `x-bili-plugin-conversation` (honored only alongside the `x-bili-plugin` marker header), then per-client headers (`x-claude-code-session-id`, `x-grok-session-id`/`x-grok-conv-id`, `x-mavis-session-id`, `x-opencode-session-id`), then generic headers (`x-session-affinity`, `x-acp-session`, `x-session-id`, `x-opencode-session`, `session-id`/`session_id`), then body fields: `session_id` / `metadata.session_id` on the Responses wire, and `prompt_cache_key` promoted over the content-fingerprint fallback on the Responses/OpenAI/Anthropic wires. | Client | Sends conversation id? | Source | |---|---|---| | **Codex** | ✅ yes | `body.session_id` / turn-metadata thread id | | **OpenCode** | ✅ yes | `x-opencode-session-id` header (`ses_…`, the request's own session id; 2.x sends the *parent's* cache-routing affinity in `x-session-affinity`/`X-Session-Id`/`x-opencode-session` alongside it, #2779 — 1.x sent its own id in those instead) | | **Claude Code** | ✅ yes | `x-claude-code-session-id` header | | **omp** (via plugin) | ✅ yes | `prompt_cache_key` promoted over any fingerprint (#268) | | **pi** (bare) | ❌ no | nothing → anonymous prefix affinity below | **omp caveat (#2583/#3556):** on recent OMP builds, default Anthropic (`anthropic-messages`) requests leave the host through OMP's Cowork transport over node:https directly — they never reach bili's fetch layer, so the `prompt_cache_key` stamp is *withheld* there (stamping would leak the field into Anthropic's strict schema → HTTP 400). Since #3556 the `bili omp` launcher lane no longer leaves that hole open by default: unless you set `PI_PROXY` / `PI_PROXY_ANTHROPIC` yourself, the launcher exports `PI_PROXY_ANTHROPIC=`, which pushes Cowork onto Bun's fetch and routes it through the proxy like every other lane (compressed and session-visible; the stamped key is consumed and stripped by the proxy). Direct-and-anonymous remains only for native omp mode and for launcher lanes where you pin your own proxy posture; all other omp traffic keeps its stamped identity. Details: [docs/technical-notes.md](docs/technical-notes.md). **omp advisor isolation (#5567):** omp's persistent background streams (e.g. a turn-reviewer *advisor* on a second model) are separate model conversations, but their Chat Completions requests carry no conversation signal of their own — the plugin stamps the main session's id into `prompt_cache_key`, so both streams land in ONE bili session. Two models/protocols interleaving into one ledger corrupts it: refs go DEAD (`cannot be anchored` / `content-changed`), fold coverage drifts, and usage/window/nudge metering cross-talks between the streams (the log line `foreign payload under a shared session id (#4805)` marks where the proxy noticed). Until the host-side identity fix lands (tracked in [#5567](https://github.com/ranxianglei/billion-context/issues/5567)), isolate the advisor by letting it carry its own identity on the wire: in omp's model-registry config (the `providers:` section of `models.yml`), set `compat.supportsPromptCacheKey: true` on the advisor's provider entry — pi-ai then serializes the advisor's own session UUID as `prompt_cache_key`, and bili binds it to its own session. Boundaries: this does not help if omp explicitly passes a shared cache key for the advisor; once isolated, the advisor runs as its own session with its own compression state; verify via the web panel that advisor traffic appears under a separate session id. **Header-less clients (pi-like): anonymous prefix affinity.** With no conversation signal at all, the proxy resolves the session from the replayed history itself (`src/prefix-affinity.ts`, #309): a request reattaches to a stored session only when its history reproduces that session's message chain byte-exactly from position 0; otherwise it gets its own deterministic `pfa-…` session. Consequences (#1262): a **resumed** conversation reattaches to its own session (even after a proxy restart, #499); a **new task with an identical opener does NOT inherit** another conversation's blocks — it mints a fresh, fully separate session; a request with no usable signal at all gets an explicit 400 instead of silently colliding. Design record and threat model: [docs/session-identity.md](docs/session-identity.md). The message-granularity sibling (why identity is content-derived, not an assigned id) is [docs/message-identity.md](docs/message-identity.md). For upstream sticky-routing, the proxy forwards only identity values the client already supplied (e.g. a body `session_id` is forwarded upstream as `x-session-id`); it never synthesizes one itself. **Recommendation:** explicit-id clients are safe to run concurrently. For header-less multi-agent use, prefer the client plugin (stamps a stable id per conversation) or pass an explicit `x-acp-session` header — otherwise prefix affinity still keeps distinct tasks apart (a diverged fork costs one raw resend plus a compression-ladder restart). ### Derived (child) sessions inherit the parent's compressed context (#1333, #1362) A child session (subagent/fork starting from an empty history) reports its lineage at birth — its identity registration carries `parentConversationId` and the proxy records a read-only `derivedFrom` link — so `decompress` / `search_context` fall back along the parent chain for content the child never saw itself (cycle-guarded, depth cap 8). Nothing is copied into the child, the parent is never modified; if the parent is unknown the child simply starts fresh. Per-lane parent signals (pi/omp `parentSession` header, OpenCode V1/V2 `parentID`): [docs/session-identity.md](docs/session-identity.md#derived-child-sessions-lineage-at-birth-1333-1362). claude/codex/dsh need nothing here: they share one session id across subagents or have no child-session concept at all. ### Running multiple instances (#3633) **One conversation belongs to one instance for its whole life.** Fold state, prefix affinity and the summary budget are keyed to a session id whose home is the client's own history — and the session's rows live in that instance's `index.db`. There is no shared store between instances: nothing replicates, nothing fails over, nothing rehydrates a session onto a different instance. Consequences for anyone tempted to put several instances behind one Service: - **Sticky routing is required, and `ClientIP` affinity is the wrong kind.** The conversation identity lives in a header or the request body, not the source IP — a Service can only hash on IP, so a client pinned to replica N silently loses *every* session when replica N dies (buying throughput while selling away availability, exactly when you scaled out because of load). Correct routing is an L7 proxy hashing a conversation header (`x-bili-plugin-conversation`, `x-opencode-session-id`, `x-acp-session`, …) onto a backend — and the client actually sending one (header-less clients get prefix affinity instead, which an L7 proxy cannot hash). - **Instance count is volume count.** The state directory is one local directory with SQLite in WAL mode (`busy_timeout=5000`); a coherent shared `-shm` and working byte-range locks across writers require an RWO volume that is never shared. Pointing two instances at the same RWX/NFS path does not give you a shared store — it gives you silent corruption behind a timeout. One RWO volume per instance, `storage.unified` included: "unified" means one store *for that instance* (sessions + CCR + CAS in one `index.db`), not one store for the fleet. - **The workload that actually scales** is *many independent short-lived conversations* — one proxy per client or per lane — not *one long conversation load-balanced across proxies*. Long conversations are single-instance by design. **Single machine, multiple installs (#5046).** The topology above covers deployment replicas; one desktop has a sibling situation: two installs on ONE machine (e.g. two DSH profiles — desktop + bot, or a global npm copy beside a host-tree copy) each start their own proxy and, unless isolated, both resolve the SAME default XDG sessions directory and the same config file. Multiple processes writing ONE local-disk `index.db` is the SUPPORTED topology (#5082/#5091) — SQLite WAL is multi-process safe on a local filesystem — so startup NEVER blocks on a live foreign writer: the peer shows up as an info-level `[storage] process pid … is also using …` line plus the status wire, nothing more (policy settled 2026-10-31, withdrawing the #5046/B-era refuse-to-start for exactly this shape). What genuinely remains hazardous is two installs walking the SAME *session* concurrently — that case alarms separately (split-brain contest, #3923). If you still want strictly separate histories and stores per install, give each its own `BILI_SESSIONS_DIR` (plus `BILI_CONFIG_FILE` when the config should differ too) through that install's launcher/profile environment — no global env changes needed. Once isolated, the `[instances]` notice drops off entirely. Note the distinction from the deployment case above: local disk with SQLite WAL tolerates many writers; shared RWX/NFS storage does NOT and keeps requiring one writer per volume. Naming note: `POST /__bili/replicas` creates a session **checkpoint fork** (from stored checkpoints), not a pod replica — read it as `/__bili/checkpoints`. The proxy rewrites each session's state file every turn of a long session; on Windows, real-time AV (Defender), the search indexer, or a sync tool (OneDrive) can lock the sessions dir mid-write, so persists fail with `EPERM` until the lock clears. Fix at the root: add `%USERPROFILE%\.local\share\billion-context\` to your antivirus exclusions (Defender steps included) and keep sync tools off that path — [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#windows-exclude-the-sessions-dir-from-antivirus-362). The same exclusion also covers the unified-storage `index.db` refusing to open (`unable to open database file`, #3823) — the storage-degrade warning names it as the first suspect. ### Session file cleanup (#1082) Short-lived sessions leave small state files behind that are never resumed. Cleanup is **opt-in** (`BILI_SESSION_GC=1`; off by default — session files are user data, no silent deletion policy): when enabled, bili sweeps the sessions dir at boot and hourly and deletes a file only when BOTH hold — older than `BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_AGE_DAYS` (default 7 days) AND never compressed with its newest request body ≤ `BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_TOKENS` tokens (default 1M) — so deletion loses nothing but bytes. CCR content stores follow their session file's lifecycle; compressed sessions are never deleted; every deletion is audit-logged. Full policy: [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#environment-variables). ### Storage maintenance CLI (#3928) The same store maintenance the panel exposes over HTTP (`POST /__bili/storage/gc`, `POST /__bili/storage/restore`) has a thin CLI layer — no proxy needed, run it on any machine that owns the sessions dir: ```bash bili sessions ls # id, label, decoded size, last-updated, storage status (active/archived) bili sessions rm # full delete (content refcount release incl. media); shrinks index.db afterwards (--no-vacuum skips) bili sessions archive # export to archive/archive.jsonl + sweep rows; tombstone keeps label & identity bili sessions restore # bring an archived session back from the log line bili sessions foreign-blocks # (#5312) list fold blocks whose covered messages never belonged to this transcript — dry-run; --apply reversibly archives them, --restore : brings one back bili storage gc [--days N] [--vacuum full|incremental] [--dry-run] # print the sweep plan (sessions past retention, zero-ref content rows, ~pages reclaimable), then run the same gc() the HTTP endpoint calls; --dry-run stops after the plan ``` `archive`/`restore`/`gc` require the unified store (`BILI_STORAGE_UNIFIED=shadow|full` or `storage.unified` in the config file) — legacy-only installs refuse with a hint. `--days` defaults to `storage.archiveAfterDays` (365). No scheduler: these run on demand. All commands accept `--json`. **Full vacuum is an offline operation on large databases (#4612).** `--vacuum full` (the default) rewrites the entire index.db under an exclusive write lock — O(db size), minutes to tens of minutes on multi-GB databases, with no intermediate progress (SQLite's VACUUM is atomic; it cannot be split). Running it while a proxy is serving from the same sessions dir starves that proxy's writes until its storage layer degrades, so `storage gc --vacuum full` **refuses to start when another live process holds the database** (`index.db.lock` pid discipline, #4175): the CLI exits 1 with an actionable message, the panel endpoint returns HTTP 409. Stop the other instance first (or wait for it to exit) and retry; for online-safe shrink use `--vacuum incremental`, which reclaims freed pages in short transactions without taking the exclusive lock. The zero-ref delete sweep itself is batched with per-batch progress output either way. ## Status Early. Protocol handling and compression work against mock tests (500+ passing). Real-model integration testing is the next milestone. Expect rough edges. Client-side plugins for pi / omp / opencode ship inside `billion-context` (`dist/agent/*.js`) for the cooperative-proxy path. See the **"Which do I need?"** section above for how `billion-context`, the standalone `billion-context-pi`, and `opencode-acp` relate. ## Attribution requirement (one term on top of MIT) This project is MIT-licensed **plus one additional term**: any product or service (commercial or open source) whose users can see or interact with it and which uses this software must attribute it — stating that it uses billion-context with a link back to this repository — on its home page, documentation, or About/Credits page. Pure server-side/embedded use satisfies this via shipped documentation. See the **Additional Term** at the end of [LICENSE](LICENSE). If you build on this project, we'd love to hear about it: open an issue (no obligation) so we can track where it's used. ## License MIT

repositories.readme:
# agent-browser Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell.

agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. `snapshot` returns the page as compact text with a ref such as `@e1` for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. ## Install ```bash npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) ``` - **Homebrew:** `brew install agent-browser`, then `agent-browser install`. - **Linux:** `agent-browser install --with-deps` also installs the browser's system libraries. - **No install:** `npx agent-browser open example.com`. Project installs, building from source, `upgrade`, and `doctor` are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation). ## Quick start ```bash agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close ``` The snapshot for `example.com`: ``` - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] ``` - Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. - CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example `agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit"`. See [Selectors](https://agent-browser.dev/selectors). - A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry. The full walkthrough is in the [quick start](https://agent-browser.dev/quick-start). ## How it works The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each `--session` gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when [session persistence](https://agent-browser.dev/sessions) is configured. Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with `--cdp` or `--auto-connect` ([CDP mode](https://agent-browser.dev/cdp-mode)), select the [Lightpanda](https://agent-browser.dev/engines/lightpanda) or [Obscura](https://agent-browser.dev/engines/obscura) engine with `--engine`, drive Mobile Safari in the [iOS Simulator](https://agent-browser.dev/ios), or use a cloud browser provider such as [Browserbase](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browserbase), [Browserless](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browserless), [Browser Use](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browser-use), [Kernel](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/kernel), or [AgentCore](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/agentcore). ## For AI agents The CLI ships skills that match its version: ```bash agent-browser skills get core # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows agent-browser skills get core --ref commands # one reference, such as the full command list agent-browser skills get core --full # adds the full command reference and templates agent-browser skills list # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more ``` Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-browser): ```bash npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser ``` The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load `agent-browser skills get core`, so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add this to your `AGENTS.md`: ```markdown Use `agent-browser` for browser automation. Before the first use, run `agent-browser skills get core` and follow it. ``` For MCP clients, `agent-browser mcp` starts an MCP server over stdio. See [MCP server](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#mcp-server). ## Commands Run `agent-browser --help` for the full list, or `agent-browser --help` for one command. | Group | Commands | Docs | |---|---|---| | Navigate and read | `open`, `back`, `forward`, `reload`, `read`, `snapshot`, `get`, `is` | [Core](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#core), [Snapshots](https://agent-browser.dev/snapshots) | | Interact | `click`, `dblclick`, `fill`, `type`, `press`, `keyboard`, `hover`, `focus`, `select`, `check`, `uncheck`, `scroll`, `drag`, `upload`, `mouse`, `find` | [Core](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#core), [Find elements](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#find-elements) | | Wait | `wait` | [Wait](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#wait) | | Capture | `screenshot`, `pdf`, `record`, `download`, `diff` | [Recording](https://agent-browser.dev/recording), [Diffing](https://agent-browser.dev/diffing), [Files](https://agent-browser.dev/files) | | Page and network state | `cookies`, `storage`, `network`, `set`, `clipboard`, `eval`, `pushstate` | [Network](https://agent-browser.dev/network), [Settings](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#settings) | | Tabs, frames, and dialogs | `tab`, `frame`, `dialog` | [Tabs and frames](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#tabs-frames) | | Debug and performance | `console`, `errors`, `highlight`, `inspect`, `trace`, `profiler`, `vitals`, `react`, `a11y` | [Debugging](https://agent-browser.dev/debugging), [Profiler](https://agent-browser.dev/profiler), [React](https://agent-browser.dev/react) | | Sessions and auth | `session`, `state`, `auth`, `profiles`, `confirm`, `deny` | [Sessions](https://agent-browser.dev/sessions), [Security](https://agent-browser.dev/security) | | Agents and integrations | `skills`, `mcp`, `webmcp`, `flow`, `chat`, `batch`, `plugin` | [Skills](https://agent-browser.dev/skills), [WebMCP](https://agent-browser.dev/webmcp), [Plugins](https://agent-browser.dev/plugins) | | Observe | `stream`, `dashboard` | [Streaming](https://agent-browser.dev/streaming), [Dashboard](https://agent-browser.dev/dashboard) | | Setup | `install`, `upgrade`, `doctor`, `connect`, `close` | [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation) | Flags, environment variables, and `agent-browser.json` are documented in [Configuration](https://agent-browser.dev/configuration). ## Platforms Native binaries ship for macOS (ARM64, x64), Linux (ARM64, x64, glibc and musl), and Windows (x64). The npm package picks the right binary for the host. ## Development Building from source requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust: ```bash pnpm install pnpm build:source # builds the dashboard and the native CLI pnpm link --global agent-browser install ``` Run the Rust checks from `cli/`: ```bash cargo fmt -- --check cargo clippy cargo test cargo test e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1 # launches real headless Chrome ``` [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) lists the files to update with each change, the docs checks, and the release process. ## Documentation - [agent-browser.dev](https://agent-browser.dev): introduction, guides, and reference - [Commands](https://agent-browser.dev/commands) and [Configuration](https://agent-browser.dev/configuration) - [Security](https://agent-browser.dev/security): the auth vault, domain allowlists, action policies, and content boundaries - [Next.js and Vercel](https://agent-browser.dev/next) and [eve](https://agent-browser.dev/eve): running agent-browser in Vercel Sandbox and eve agents - [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) ## License Apache-2.0

# 云析桌面版 · YunX-Desktop **粘贴分享链接，直接高速下载 —— 云析 YunX 官方 Windows 桌面版** 网盘：夸克 / UC / 迅雷 / 百度 / 139 / 123 / 115 / 光鸭 / 蓝奏云 / 蓝奏云优享版； 视频：哔哩哔哩 / 小红书 / 抖音 / 微博 / 快手 / AcFun / Pixiv；另支持磁力 / BT 种子 / ed2k 等 P2P 链接。 Range 分片并发 + 断点续传，B 站高清自动合轨。 [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/tidain/YunX-Desktop?style=flat-square\&label=release\&color=4C8BF5)](https://github.com/tidain/YunX-Desktop/releases/latest) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/tidain/YunX-Desktop?style=flat-square\&logo=github\&color=4C8BF5)](https://github.com/tidain/YunX-Desktop/stargazers) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-AGPL--3.0-blue?style=flat-square)](./LICENSE) [![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-0078D6?style=flat-square\&logo=windows\&logoColor=white)](#构建) [![Kotlin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kotlin-7F52FF?style=flat-square\&logo=kotlin\&logoColor=white)](https://kotlinlang.org/) [![Compose](https://img.shields.io/badge/Compose%20Multiplatform-Desktop-4285F4?style=flat-square\&logo=jetpackcompose\&logoColor=white)](https://www.jetbrains.com/lp/compose-multiplatform/) [下载最新版](https://github.com/tidain/YunX-Desktop/releases/latest) · [功能](docs/FEATURES.md) · [使用](docs/USAGE.md) · [浏览器插件](#浏览器插件) · [构建](docs/BUILD.md) · [常见问题](#常见问题) · [与安卓版差异](docs/UPSTREAM-DIFF.md)
*** > **云析永远免费开源。** 如果你是在任何地方「花钱买到」的，说明你被骗了，请立即退款。 > 任何收费版本均为二次打包的诈骗版本，与本项目无关。 > **本项目使用 AGPL-3.0 开源协议。** 与安卓版 [CYQawa/YunX](https://github.com/CYQawa/YunX) > 同属云析项目；若你使用了本项目的代码，请同样以 AGPL-3.0 开放源代码。 ## 简介 云析 YunX 的 **官方 Windows 桌面版**：粘贴**网盘分享链接**或**视频作品链接**，即可浏览内容、在线预览并直接高速下载，全程在电脑上完成； 也支持**磁力 / BT 种子 / ed2k** 等 P2P 链接下载。 网盘与视频平台都支持多账号（主账号 / 备注），登录凭证加密存本机，并可导出加密备份换机恢复。 提供**免安装便携版**（整个文件夹拷走即用）与**安装版**（开始菜单 / 桌面快捷方式，可卸载）两种分发形式。 ## 截图 | | | | :------------------------------------------------------: | :--------------------------------------------------------: | | | | | 主界面 | 网盘登录 | | | | | 设置 | 关于 | ## 支持平台 - 夸克网盘 - UC 网盘 - 迅雷网盘 - 百度网盘 - 139 网盘（和彩云） - 123 云盘 - 115 网盘 - 光鸭云盘 - 蓝奏云 / 蓝奏云优享版 - GitHub（仓库 / 账号 / 文件直链） - 视频解析：抖音 / 快手 / 微博 / 小红书 / 哔哩哔哩 / AcFun / Pixiv - 磁力 / BT 种子 / ed2k（P2P 下载，可导入本地种子文件） > \[!WARNING] > **不建议使用百度网盘，可能导致账号被风控！** ## 浏览器插件 仓库 `browser-extension/` 内含 Chrome / Edge 扩展「**云析下载助手**」（Manifest V3）—— 让浏览器下载接管到云析的多线程下载。 - **嗅探页面资源**：列出当前网页里可下载的媒体与文件，按图片 / 视频 / 音频 / 文档 / 压缩包 / 程序 / 字体分类，图片与视频支持卡片预览。 - **接管浏览器下载**：浏览器开始下载时自动接管（取消浏览器下载并抹掉记录），由云析弹窗询问保存目录与线程数（最高 512，超过 32 需二次确认）。 - **归还浏览器下载**：点「归还浏览器下载」后重新发起浏览器原生下载，并对该页面网站（根域名及其子域名）写入 **5 分钟冷却**；冷却期内打开插件可看到「还有 X 分 YY 秒」倒计时，并可点「立即重新开始」单独解除当前网站的冷却。 - **视频平台卡片**：B 站视频页可选清晰度与下载方式；抖音 / 微博 / AcFun 视频页可一键交给云析解析下载。 - **安全**：扩展与云析通过本机回环 HTTP（`127.0.0.1`，随机 token）通信，网页脚本无法伪造请求；**云析没运行时探测不到端口，扩展完全不干预浏览器下载**。 安装、开关与工作原理见 [浏览器插件说明](browser-extension/README.md)。 ## 功能 - **分享链接解析** —— 识别夸克 / UC / 迅雷 / 百度 / 139 / 123 / 115 / 光鸭 / 蓝奏云 / 蓝奏云优享版 分享链接并自动匹配提取码，另支持 GitHub 仓库 / 账号 / 文件直链 - **视频解析与预览** —— 粘贴抖音 / 快手 / 微博 / 小红书 / B站 / AcFun / Pixiv 作品链接（短链、口令、整段文案均可）即可解析；在线预览优先用 **ffplay** 直读直链（真·边下边播，HLS 原生支持），本机没装 FFmpeg 时回退内置播放器并可一键下载引擎到应用私有目录（不改系统环境变量）；图集可放大查看，下载支持 DASH 合轨（优先 ffmpeg `-c copy`）与 Live Photo 动图合成（可存动态照片 / 静图 / 视频） - **高速下载** —— Range 分片并发 + 断点续传 + 慢连接自动换线 + 全局限速；B 站高清分轨两轨并行下载后自动合轨 - **P2P 下载** —— 磁力 / BT 种子 / ed2k 电驴链接交给 Gopeed 引擎下载；支持导入本地 `.torrent` 种子文件、BT Tracker 服务器二级页管理与 DHT 开关，下载中可查看「种子 / 连接 / 节点」概览 - **GitHub 浏览与 README 渲染** —— 浏览仓库文件树 / Releases / 账号仓库列表，README 与更新说明以 GFM Markdown 渲染 - **GitHub 下载镜像自动测速** —— 内置五个 gh-proxy 系镜像，下载前并发实测每个镜像的延迟与下载速度，按速度自动选最快（设置页可看 ping / 速度、手动刷新、固定某个或自定义前缀），更新包 / 视频引擎 / Gopeed 内核 / README 图片统一走该镜像 - **通知中心进度** —— 下载进度实时显示为 Windows 通知中心 toast 进度条（多任务聚合 + 实时速度） - **多种登录方式** —— 内嵌 Chromium 登录 / 一键导入本机浏览器 Cookie / 手动粘贴 Cookie；GitHub 可选 Personal Access Token - **Windows 系统集成** —— 原生托盘菜单（亮暗跟随系统配色）、原生文件对话框、剪贴板分享链接检测 - **多账号与认证备份** —— 网盘与视频平台都支持多账号（主账号 / 备注 / 逐个退出）；「设置 → 认证备份」可加密导出 / 导入全部账号，换机免重登 - **桌面体验** —— 深色模式 + 自定义种子色、链接收藏、解析历史、窗口内弹窗覆盖层 - **网络** —— GitHub 下载镜像（自动测速选最快 / 固定预选 / 自定义前缀）、HTTP 代理（便于加速或直连受限的场景） - **引擎管理** —— 下载引擎（Gopeed 内核）与视频预览引擎（FFmpeg 精简版）集中管理，可下载 / 更新 / 卸载并查看路径与来源 完整功能清单见 **[功能清单](docs/FEATURES.md)**。 ## 与安卓版的差异 桌面版在**登录方式、系统集成（托盘 / 通知 / 原生对话框）、数据存储、构建分发**上针对 Windows 做了适配， 并移除了移动端专属功能。完整清单见 **[与安卓版的差异](docs/UPSTREAM-DIFF.md)**。 ## 技术栈 | 分类 | 选型 | | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | 语言 | Kotlin | | UI | Compose Multiplatform（Desktop）+ Material 3 | | 持久化 | `sqlite-jdbc`（SQLite）+ `java.util.prefs` | | 网络 | OkHttp 4.12.0（请求 + 分片下载） | | 内嵌浏览器 | JCEF 132（Chromium） | | 视频预览 | ffplay（FFmpeg 套件，边下边播）+ JavaFX Media（兜底） | | 原生桥接 | JNA（Win32 API）+ 自编 `darkmode.dll` | | 构建分发 | Gradle + jlink + jpackage + Inno Setup | | Markdown 渲染 | multiplatform-markdown-renderer（GFM：README / 更新说明） | ## 使用 1. 在「网盘」页登录需要使用的网盘账号（推荐内嵌浏览器登录）；视频解析平台的登录在「解析」页对应平台卡片或结果页里完成 2. 在「解析」页粘贴分享链接或视频链接（可带提取码，支持从剪贴板一键粘贴） 3. 网盘分享会进入文件浏览页，视频链接会进入结果页（可选清晰度 / 图集 / 预览） 4. 在「下载」页查看进度，支持暂停 / 继续 / 删除 / 打开；进度同步显示在 Windows 通知中心 设置项、数据目录、托盘操作见 **[使用说明](docs/USAGE.md)**。 ## 构建 要求：Windows 10/11 x64，另需一个 **C++ 编译器**（托盘菜单配色桥接层用；缺它时 `run` / `package` / `installer` 会在这一步失败）。JDK、Gradle、Inno Setup 均无需手动安装。 ```powershell git clone https://github.com/tidain/YunX-Desktop.git cd YunX-Desktop .\run.ps1 run # 编译并启动（开发，含 darkmode.dll） .\run.ps1 build # 仅编译 Kotlin（不需要 C++ 编译器） .\run.ps1 package # 免安装便携版 → release\YunX-Desktop\ .\run.ps1 installer # 单文件安装程序 → release\YunX-Desktop-setup-*.exe ``` 环境要求、版本号管理与打包产物见 **[构建与打包](docs/BUILD.md)**。 ## 常见问题
为什么从「第三方移植」变成了「官方桌面版」？ 项目早期确实是社区移植（安卓版 [CYQawa/YunX](https://github.com/CYQawa/YunX) 的 Windows 移植）。 **2026 年 10 月 2 日上午 8:40**，桌面版作者（tidain）加入安卓版仓库成为协作者， 桌面版自此与安卓版同属一个项目，作为云析的**官方 Windows 桌面端**维护； 两端的代码、发布节奏与分发方式仍各自独立。
百度网盘下载 / 转存不了？ 账号被风控了，详见安卓版 issue #9。
便携版和安装版有什么区别？ 便携版是免安装的文件夹，拷到任意位置双击 `YunX-Desktop.exe` 即可运行； 安装版走安装向导，安装到 `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\YunX-Desktop`，并创建开始菜单 / 桌面快捷方式，可在设置中卸载。 两者功能完全一致。
下载时看不到 Windows 通知中心的通知？ 先确认「设置 → 系统 → 通知」已开启（专注助手 / 免打扰也会拦通知）。应用在检测到通知未送达时， 会尝试自动创建所需的开始菜单快捷方式兜底，但最终能否弹出仍取决于系统通知设置。
## 支持开发 - **GitHub Star**：给 [tidain/YunX-Desktop](https://github.com/tidain/YunX-Desktop) 点个 Star ⭐ - **提交 Issues**：发现 Bug 或有功能建议欢迎反馈 - **赞赏**：应用内「支持开发」页面可扫码赞赏安卓版作者（CYQawa）与桌面端作者（tidain） ## 文档 | 文档 | 内容 | | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | | [功能清单](docs/FEATURES.md) | 全部功能与细节 | | [使用说明](docs/USAGE.md) | 快速上手、登录方式、设置项、数据目录、托盘操作 | | [构建与打包](docs/BUILD.md) | 环境要求、命令、版本号、打包产物、目录结构 | | [与安卓版的差异](docs/UPSTREAM-DIFF.md) | 桌面版相对安卓版的新增 / 重做 / 移除 | | [免责声明](docs/DISCLAIMER.md) | 免责声明、协议逆向说明、反倒卖、开源协议 | ## 开源协议 本项目与安卓版 [CYQawa/YunX](https://github.com/CYQawa/YunX) 同属云析项目，同样以 [GNU AGPL-3.0](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html) 协议开源，详见 [LICENSE](LICENSE)。 完整的免责与合规说明见 **[免责声明](docs/DISCLAIMER.md)**。 ## 更多 - 安卓版仓库： - PC 版仓库： - 问题与建议： ## 友情链接 - 云析的Docker社区移植版（基于本仓库修改，作为本仓库的下游分支）：[mu-zi-lee/YunX-Docker](https://github.com/mu-zi-lee/YunX-Docker) ## 贡献者 Contributors ## Star History
